text: You've already planned capacity for web tiers and databases, where scaling out almost always just works. GPUs break that assumption. A specific high-demand accelerator in a specific region is a physically constrained resource — the provider only has so many racked, powered, and networked at once. When demand is high, a request for more can fail outright, not slowly, and no amount of money fixes that in the next five minutes. That's why GPU capacity planning has to be anticipatory, not reactive.

A workable cycle has four real steps. Forecast GPU-hour demand from your training and inference roadmap further ahead than feels natural. File quota increase requests against that forecast with genuine lead time. Reserve capacity for the runs that are large, time-boxed, and already committed to. And build a fallback hierarchy for everything else — a preferred SKU, a next-best SKU or region, and, where the workload tolerates it, a degraded CPU-only path instead of an outright failure.

The first wall you hit is usually your own account's quota, not the data center's hardware. Azure and AWS both cap how many instances of a GPU family your subscription can provision in a region by default, independent of whether physical capacity exists at all. Checking that quota and filing an increase request is straightforward — az vm list-usage on Azure, or a Service Quotas lookup on AWS — but approval doesn't guarantee the hardware is actually sitting there waiting once it lands.

Once you know you need a GPU family at a predictable time, you can trade flexibility for a guarantee. Azure On-Demand Capacity Reservations hold a specific VM size in a specific zone, billed whether or not you're running on it. AWS Capacity Blocks for ML reserve a cluster of GPU instances for a defined future window, built for a known training run. Both are the GPU-era version of what reserved instances already do for cost — except here the thing you're buying is availability itself.

Reservations make the most sense for forecastable, high-stakes demand — a quarter's training roadmap, a launch date you've already committed to — not every GPU need a team has. Combine forecasting, early quota requests, targeted reservations, and a real fallback hierarchy, and a capacity shortfall becomes a planned degradation instead of an incident. Next lesson turns to the regional side of the same problem: why training and inference genuinely need different multi-region strategies.
